implementation_notes: On the JVM the JDK collections are used directly: CopyOnWriteArrayList and CopyOnWriteArraySet copy the backing array on every mutation, so reads and iteration are lock-free snapshots - the default when a listener list or small registry is read far more often than written. Kotlin adds the value-level style on top: read-only List/Map/Set interfaces and copy() on data classes give non-destructive updates of a state holder, and the type system shows that the returned value is a new one rather than a mutated original.
code_sketch:
private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Listener>()

fun subscribe(l: Listener) = listeners.add(l)      // copies the array
fun fire(e: Event) = listeners.forEach { it.on(e) } // snapshot iteration

data class Settings(val host: String, val port: Int)
fun withPort(s: Settings, p: Int) = s.copy(port = p) // new value
pitfalls: CopyOnWriteArrayList.add in a loop is quadratic and allocates per element; build a List once and construct the collection from it.
Iterators are snapshots: a listener registered during iteration is not called, and removals during iteration are simply unseen.
data class copy() is shallow: a MutableList field shared between copies reintroduces aliasing.

variants.name: kotlinx.collections.immutable persistent collections
variants.implementation_notes: For structure-level sharing, kotlinx.collections.immutable provides immutable and persistent collections whose plus/minus operations may share storage with the original, plus builder and mutate helpers when many changes must be applied at once; the read-only Kotlin interfaces make the immutability visible in the type system. Prefer this over JVM copy-on-write collections when the data is a state value consumed by UI or reducers rather than a registration list, and on multiplatform targets where java.util.concurrent is unavailable.
variants.code_sketch:
import kotlinx.collections.immutable.*

val base: PersistentList<Item> = persistentListOf(Item("a"))
val next = base.add(Item("b"))                 // shares storage with base
val also = base.mutate { it.add(Item("c")) }   // builder for many changes
pitfalls: The library is an Alpha-stage external dependency (kotlinx-collections-immutable); these interfaces are not in the Kotlin standard library.
toImmutableList() returns the receiver itself when it is already immutable, so mutating through another reference to that same object is still the caller's bug.
Persistent updates pay O(log n) path copying, so a hot loop should batch changes through builder/mutate.
